newsitem.title: USA: Time Warner hires financial adviser for New Line.
newsitem.headline: Time Warner hires financial adviser for New Line.

text.p: Time Warner Inc., after receiving regulators' permission last week to proceed with its acquisiton of Turner Broadcasting System Inc., has retained Wall Street firm Furman Selz to advise on strategic alternatives for TBS' New Line Cinema, Time Warner sources say.

Furman's job is not to oversee an outright sale of the studio, but to review the different options -- ranging from sale of a minority or a majority stake or equity alliance with a strategic partner, the sources told Variety. Neither Time Warner, TBS nor Furman Selz would comment.
Unlike TBS' other studio, Castle Rock Entertainment, whose sale is now being negotiated, New Line is a success story and Turner has reportedly been reluctant to sell it.
But New Line Chairman Robert Shaye is reluctant to report to Warner Bros. co-chairmen Bob Daly and Terry Semel, which he may have had to do if New Line were integrated into Warner Bros.

But Warner Bros. wants to retain a strategic link to New Line. Furman's job will be to come up with a structure that allows Time Warner to get some value out of New Line, while ensuring Shaye retains some independence.

"The range of options is broad," said one source, from selling 20 percent to the public to selling 51 percent or bringing in a partner. Taking the company public would also ensure it had independent access to capital.
The decision to focus on these options is believed to have the support of Turner, Time Warner Chairman Gerald Levin, Shaye and Warner Bros.

Wall Streeters predict Time Warner will find plenty of interest in New Line, particularly if the strategic partner option is pursued. "You will find a lot of the people who looked at MGM -- domestic and international players -- figure this is a better distribution company than MGM," one banker said.

One of the big questions is how much New Line is worth. It was sold to TBS in 1993 for about $550 million, but entertainment bankers say it is worth more than $750 million now. Since being acquired by TBS, the company has expanded its production slate and the budget of its pictures, and many of the subsequent releases, such as "Seven," have been big hits.
The selection of Furman is not surprising as the firm was New Line's longtime banker and advised the company on its sale to TBS.
